articleTitle: The effect of recent advances in computer technology on dynamic process simulation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Cost Effective Industrial Simulation
abstract: As process plants are inherently time varying, dynamic simulation can provide insight and solutions not available through other techniques, for example in the following areas: safety and environmental aspects, process and control design, operation optimisation, and training and education. The use of modern simulation methods has led to the following trends: replacement of older simulation systems with newer interactive general purpose systems; broadening user base; cheaper simulation projects, faster turn around and more reliable results; and greater model complexity and size.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Simulation-a through life benefit to equipment operators
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Cost Effective Industrial Simulation
abstract: When considering the appropriate level of analysis to apply at any particular stage in a project it is necessary to consider what information is needed by whom and when. Thus the project management plan, is an essential tool in making this assessment. It enables the decision to be made in the light of the overall needs of the project rather than from the view point associated with an isolated phase in the project. This principle applies both when considering developing a new piece of equipment and throughout its service life. It also applies when modifying it and is illustrated by reference to the author's experience at Frazer-Nash in the design of articulated vehicles. However some of the considerations that need to be taken into account when deciding the appropriate level of modelling to be used at each stage in a project are set out first. The advantages of computer simulation in project development are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Cost Effective Industrial Simulation
abstract: In the contracting business simulation plays an increasingly important role in tendering and project execution in the evaluation of alternatives and assessing the risks associated with solutions. The benefits and financial savings generated by simulation come from direct labour, capital investment, productivity improvements (and savings in) overheads and materials. Once armed with the knowledge of the benefits that may be achieved, the managers next step should be in quantifying what it will cost to generate a model that will produce adequate results on which to base a decision; this is done together with the systems modeller. A spreadsheet is used to calculate the duration of such a modelling task. Other aspects of managing a simulation model for contracting businesses are also presented.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Cost Effective Industrial Simulation
abstract: Cost justification of manufacturing simulation projects is difficult for several reasons which are listed. The author goes on to give advice on how to reduce the costs in using simulation for manufacturing process planning. An outline of expected costs is given and various management tips are given.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Cost conscious design of power supply equipment using a simulator
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Cost Effective Industrial Simulation
abstract: A multi-train simulator developed at the University of Birmingham has been used for the Central Line renewal programme and other railway systems. This system has been purchased by London Underground. Further development of the simulator is required for the Northern Line. As a result, a project was initiated by the Development Directorate to develop the simulator. The project is being undertaken by the London Underground Design Consultancy Group-Professional Services Group operating within the Engineering Directorate. The authors outline the interaction of the three parties (client, client engineer and professional services) concerned with the simulator, how the simulator will be used, the work involved in extending its capabilities and the cost justification for the simulator development programme.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Cost Effective Industrial Simulation
abstract: A rapid increase in the use and application of analysis simulation has occurred. With increasing power of computers and relative decreasing hardware costs, the use of these methods within the design process has become more common. Finite element analysis is typical of many advanced analysis tools such as computational fluid dynamics, boundary methods and control simulation and is used as an example. The finite element method is within easy reach of most engineers performing day to day tasks. Now that such analysis methods are more freely available to engineers, they need to be aware of the possible stumbling blocks they are likely to encounter which will influence both analysis timescales and costs. Some 'at the coalface analysis' guidelines have been developed based on experience gained in using the finite element method closely linked with the design process. The guidelines are categorised as follows: general ground rules, analysis choice, upgrades, input, (preprocessing), computer resources, output, (post-processing), software integration, training and risks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A dynamic, statistical and fiscal model for a hardboard mill
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Cost Effective Industrial Simulation
abstract: There are three things a company must do to compete effectively. They are to: provide an efficient well automated manufacturing system which will give the business a distinct advantage over competitors; determine the order-winning-criteria (OWC); and control the process in such a way that the product meets the order winning criteria and maximises profit. It is not sufficient to control the process alone. It is essential to ensure that there is a degree of fit between marketing strategy and manufacturing ability. Having established that fit, it is essential to ensure that the process operates in the most profitable way possible. The authors describe how elements of a hardboard mill were instrumented and automated. They also explains how a real-time dynamic, fiscal and statistical computer mill model was produced. The purpose of the model is to enable the mill manager to meet the OWC and maximise profit.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
